study.title: Ezekiel 7 The end has come to the earth and to its leaders
study.overview: Ezekiel 7 announces, with intentional repetition and solemn tone, that God's judgment on the land of Israel is not a historical accident, but a divine sentence already determined. The chapter insists that the end is near, after violence, idolatry, pride and injustice have filled the earth. The result is total: useless wealth, profane worship, powerless leadership and people without direction. The text culminates in the affirmation that through his ways the Lord will be recognized as the one who judges.

outline.title: The announcement of the end and the certainty of judgment
outline.explanation: The word of the LORD comes as a decree: the end came upon all the earth, and the judgment will be according to the ways of the people. There is no divine indecision or space for religious self-preservation; the people will see that the LORD is just in punishing his abominations.

outline.title: The incomparable calamity is already in motion
outline.explanation: The prophet repeats that disaster comes without delay. The emphasis is not only on suffering, but on the irreversible character of the sentence: the wrath of God will be poured out, compassion not suspended by human merit, and the people themselves will know the LORD as the one who hurts in judgment.

outline.title: The superb flourished, but nothing can save
outline.explanation: Violence springs from pride, and the entire social order collapses: buying and selling lose meaning, war is not successfully realized, the sword, the famine and the plague reap the men, and the survivors are unforsaken. Wealth, silver, and gold are useless before the day of wrath, because they have become a stumbling block of wickedness.

outline.title: The desecrated sanctuary and the silenced leadership
outline.explanation: External glory becomes a motive for pride and idolatry, so God surrenders what was precious to desecration for foreigners. Then the chain symbolizes the captivity and the blood-filled city receives its judgments. In the end, kings, princes, and the whole people are terrified; there will be no peace, no prophetic direction, nor priestly council or of the elders who can reverse the decree.

study.context: The chapter presents itself as an oracle of judgment pronounced through Ezekiel against the land of Israel/Judah, in language of intense repetition and strong images. The notes provided highlight that the destruction announced is not random, but a result of the Lord's judgment on the accumulated sin of the people. They also appear allusions to captivity, to the profanation of the sanctuary and to the collapse of civil and religious leaderships. The biblical text itself is sufficient to show that the scenario is of total national crisis, with judgment reaching city, field, temple and government.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter emphasizes the holiness and righteousness of God. Sin is not treated as mere social error, but as an abomination before the Lord, demanding proportional judgment. There is also a strong doctrine of the uselessness of false support: wealth, prestige, fortifications, rites, and human authority do not deliver when God decides to judge. Another central point is the knowledge of God through judgment: the text repeatedly concludes that the people will know that the Lord is the one who acts. This shows that divine judgment is not whim, but a revelation of the holy character of God before a nation that persisted in violence, idolatry, and pride. The passage also teaches that when the light of God is rejected, even the means of guidance to the priest, prophet, counsel can cease as an expression of God's judicial abandonment.

scholarViews.insight: The chapter presents three messages of judgment, and the range grows to encompass the whole earth; judgment is no longer only imminent, but has arrived.
Destruction is described as final, complete and universal, because the sin that brought it was also universal; leaders and people will be equally without hope of direction.
The king and the people would be taken into captivity, and the order of the chapter includes the symbolic imprisonment by the current as a sign of future slavery.

questions: What forms of false security money, position, external religion or self-confidence appear in this chapter as incapable of saving?
How will the repetition that the people will know that I am the LORD corrects a superficial vision of God in times of crisis?
How can our community life avoid violence, pride and indifference that appear as the cause of judgment?
study.practice: Read this chapter as called to sincere repentance and not as curiosity about disasters. Confess areas in which you have trusted in resources that cannot sustain the soul. Seek justice, humility, and practical reverence before God, remembering that the text shows that judgment begins when sin is tolerated and the voice of God is despised. In concrete terms, examine your finances, your words and your relationships: where there is pride, verbal violence, injustice or functional idolatry, abandon this and ask the Lord for an obedient heart.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not accurately detail the complete historical context, the exact date of the oracle or the geographical references outside the text itself. There are also variations of translation between the presented Bible and the notes; therefore, the reading was done only based on the content provided, without appealing to external information or for speculative reconstructions.
